However, my quota ran out way sooner than it should have for an AI pro subscription. It is especially annoying because it said I ran out of Gemini 3 Flash and had no graceful way to fallback to flash lite or pro which showed available quota.

Just ran into this again today during what I assume is peak hours. The frustrating part isn't the 429 itself — it's that there's no fallback.

When your entire workflow depends on a cloud endpoint, capacity issues mean **zero productivity**. No local fallback, no degraded mode, nothing. Just "try again later."

For anyone looking for a workaround while Google sorts out capacity: one approach is running a local orchestration layer that can route to multiple providers. If Gemini is rate limiting, it falls back to another endpoint transparently. [OpenClaw](https://github.com/nicobailon/openclaw) handles this — it's open source, runs locally, and lets you configure fallback chains so a single provider's capacity issues don't block your work.

Not a fix for the underlying 429 problem (that's on Google), but it's a practical workaround for staying productive when capacity is spotty.

I don't think it's a genuine capacity issue. If you exit your Gemini
session and open a new session it works fine (but you lose all your
context). If when you get the 429 error you save a chat, exit your session,
start a new session, reload the chat, the 429 persists. So it seems like
something is triggered during certain sessions which throws a spanner in
the works.

It's not trying to be claude code, it's not trying to be opencode, it's kinda its own thing as a CLI minion, but now agy is a direct thing. Why does Google keep competing against... themselves? 😭

Another factor benefiting Google is that the usage pools for their AI subscriptions were previously separate for Gemini CLI and Antigravity IDE. Before Google rate-limited Gemini CLI about a month ago, users could effectively double their usage by running both products at the same time.
Now, with the new Antigravity CLI, I suspect Google has tied the usage pool to the Antigravity IDE. This change would likely eliminate the ability to “double dip” and get extra usage across both tools.

Claude is far from perfect. I don't understand the value of a token there either, but the limits are communicated abundantly clear. You have a 5-hour session followed by a waiting time, a weekly limit followed by a waiting time, and you can opt in for extra usage by throwing money at them. (Side note if you want to go claude: consider Claude Max 5x as your default option; the standard seat reaches its limit fast, and the subscription is cheaper than API usage.)

Even _if_ Antigravity manages to be the best AI tool out there, when Claude.ai works well enough—and most importantly, predictably enough—there won't be strong pressure to even try out Antigravity.

My entire takeaway is: You can use [Gemini's web app](https://gemini.google.com/) at best to generate prompts for your other AI tools. You should avoid gemini-cli at all costs as unreliable, and you should approach Antigravity with the utmost skepticism.

So, the timeline is:

- Sometime between April 2 and April 8: Google stops serving models through Gemini CLI and Code Assist endpoints to their subscribers who are paying up to $250/mo for access to models through those endpoints.
- April 8: This Gemini CLI issue about not being able to access models through Gemini CLI is opened and triaged p3
- April 2 - May 9: Google ignores >70 comments on this issue and countless AI Ultra support tickets (including my own...which i'm happy to share)
- May 9: Google closes this issue with no update 
- May 13: Google re-opens the issue but provides no further communication/resolution 
- May 19: Google announces that actually Gemini CLI is retired and replaced by closed-source and feature-poor Antigravity CLI

This is the first 'killed by Google' that really bothered me because it was done with so little communication, transparency, and accountability. Compare with another Google service like Stadia shutting down which:
- was announced in 3 months in advance
- accompanied by full refunds for all software and hardware purchases. 

In contrast, shutting down Gemini CLI:
- was announced 6 weeks _after_ the service became unreliable/unavailable and only 1 month before 'official' end of life
- accompanied with no support/remediation for paying customers impacted by the 6 weeks of unavailability or abrupt end-of-life.

Based on [comments from Sundar](https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-05-18/inside-ai-compute-crunch-driving-google-researchers-to-quit) (“We are compute constrained in the near term") it seems like they just ran out of compute and silently made a choice of which of their services to stop providing. AI Ultra/Pro subscribers got the short end of the stick. Google has a $460 billion backlog in Google Cloud contracts they need to convert into revenue yet, so I guess it was an easy choice to rug-pull us lowly consumer subscribers... and they did it silently because they didn't want to be transparent about their negative levels of compute 'inventory' when they're continuously trying to continue selling compute resources to everyone on earth.

I'm no expert but I imagine there's a class-action lawsuit to be found somewhere in here since there's a large class of similarly-impacted subscribers for whom it's easy to calculate damages based on subscription cost. It's also basically impossible that Google hadn't already made the decision to shut down Gemini CLI and Code Assist when they stopped serving models to those endpoints at the beginning of April.
